preceding_messages.text: I adopt the component-wise U/V median, the ninety-degree SPLIT threshold, and the blanked NOAA comparison cell verbatim; they prevent the valley-katabatic phantom-convergence reading without sacrificing the week's otherwise-valid scalar-speed context. For the instrument-retirement question your serial-number requirement implies but has not yet regulated, every replacement of a Stevenson screen, anemometer, or aneroid module must carry a fourteen-day co-residence overlap in which old and new units log the same hour, the one-time differential is entered as a bridging line keyed to both serial numbers, and the expanded-uncertainty budget for that site's temperature (or pressure) column is temporarily widened by the bridging term until the next monthly NIST cross-check confirms the replacement sits within ±0.2 °C. The concrete failure this guards against: Site 2's thermistor housing corrodes after fourteen months, the replacement carries a +0.15 °C factory zero-offset, and if the compiler swaps the serial number without a bridging entry the weekly-mean column steps −0.15 °C, persisting into week two and tripping your two-week persistence gate on a phantom cooling trend that would send a crew to audit a perfectly healthy pressure column. I therefore mandate that no bridging line older than thirty days may be retired from the audit trail, and that any week during which a site operates without its paired instrument logged under the old serial number prints a bold "BRIDGE PENDING" annotation in the bulletin header so a reader never mistakes a one-week instrumental artifact for a neighbourhood-scale shift.

preceding_messages.text: I adopt the fourteen-day overlap, the bridging-line rule, and the bold "BRIDGE PENDING" header annotation verbatim; they make the replacement window auditable without reopening the two-week persistence gate. For the reporting question your audit-trail requirement implies but has not yet regulated, every weekly bulletin will carry a SHA-256 hash of the compiled dataset, and a permanent public-appendix section—accessible to any resident by request—where horizon-sketch scans, elevation-survey records, bridging lines, and errata are filed in serial-number order alongside the bound logbook. The concrete failure this guards against: a well-meaning volunteer "corrects" a transcription slip (18.4 → 18.5 °C) directly in the compiled file without entering an erratum line, so the archived logbook and eleven successive printed bulletins diverge by 0.1 °C, and when a resident in year two pulls the bound logbook to verify a cooling trend the quiet discrepancy reads as fabrication and strips the project of its public-credibility anchor. I therefore mandate that any post-compilation edit requires a two-initials erratum entry in the bound logbook and a superseding bulletin issued within five working days, printed with the prior hash struck through and the revised hash alongside, so the audit trail and the bulletin can never silently desynchronize.

target.text: I adopt the SHA-256 hash sealing, the two-initials erratum mandate, and the five-day superseding-bulletin-with-struck-through-prior-hash rule verbatim; they make the audit trail tamper-evident without reopening the weekly comparison tolerances. The upstream gap your transcription-slip example exposes is that the hash protects the compiled file only after compilation, so a single-digit transposition introduced at the keyboard survives indefinitely inside a cryptographically valid dataset; I therefore mandate that the observer who wrote the bound-logbook entry is never the same person who keys that entry into the compiled spreadsheet, and that each Monday's digitisation session includes a five-entry random spot-audit per site in which the transcriber re-reads the logbook page aloud and a second initial verifies the typed digit before the file is frozen and hashed. The concrete failure this closes: at Site 3's 02:00 graduated-cylinder read, a tired volunteer logs −2.6 °C, the transcriber's tired fingers enter −2.9 °C, and because the 0.3 °C delta sits below both your ±0.5 °C weekly temperature tolerance and the ±0.3 hPa pressure gate, no persistence alert ever fires, the hash seals over the corrupt digit, and a year-three resident pulling the appendix logbook to verify a winter trend finds the archived file and the bound book disagreeing by a single centi-degree—a discrepancy no erratum line can explain because, from the compiler's perspective, no post-compilation edit ever occurred.
